title: Existential crisis — Meaning, Genes, And Nothing Else
description:
Existential crisis did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Existential crises are inner conflicts characterized by the impression that life lacks meaning and by confusion about one's personal identity. They are accompanied by anxiety and stress, often to such a degree that they disturb one's normal functioning in everyday life and lead to depression.

Nobody designed the part of Existential crisis you experience — it was inherited. The main cognitive aspect of existential crises is the loss of meaning and purpose. In this context, the term "meaninglessness" refers to the general impression that there is no higher significance, direction, or purpose in our actions or in the world at large.

Emotional components refer to the feelings such as emotional pain, despair, helplessness, guilt, anxiety, or loneliness.

Cognitive components encompass the problem of meaninglessness, the loss of personal values or spiritual faith, and thinking about death. Existential crises may occur at different stages in life: the teenage crisis, the quarter-life crisis, the mid-life crisis, and the later-life crisis.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Existential crisis shows exactly where that breaks. Earlier crises tend to be forward-looking: the individual is anxious and confused about which path in life to follow regarding education, career, personal identity, and social relationships. Often triggered by the impression that one is past one's peak in life, they are usually characterized by guilt, regret, and a fear of death.

What looks like free choice in Existential crisis is older than choice itself. If an earlier existential crisis was properly resolved, it is easier for the individual to resolve or avoid later crises. The problem of meaninglessness plays a central role in all of these types.

Nobody designed the part of Existential crisis you experience — it was inherited. It can arise in the form of cosmic meaning, which is concerned with the meaning of life at large or why we are here. Another form concerns personal secular meaning, in which the individual tries to discover purpose and value mainly for their own life.

Every serious account of Existential crisis eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Finding a source of meaning may resolve a crisis, like altruism, dedicating oneself to a religious or political cause, or finding a way to develop one's potential. Other approaches include adopting a new system of meaning, learning to accept meaninglessness, cognitive behavioral therapy, and the practice of social perspective-taking.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Existential crisis — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Negative consequences of existential crisis include anxiety and bad relationships on the personal level as well as a high divorce rate and decreased productivity on the social level. Some questionnaires, such as the Purpose in Life Test, measure whether someone is currently undergoing an existential crisis.

The selfish-gene reading of Existential crisis makes it less romantic and far more precise. Outside its main use in psychology and psychotherapy, the term "existential crisis" refers to a threat to the existence of something. In psychology and psychotherapy, the term "existential crisis" refers to a form of inner conflict.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. It is characterized by the impression that life lacks meaning and is accompanied by various negative experiences, such as stress, anxiety, despair, and depression. This often happens to such a degree that it disturbs one's normal functioning in everyday life.

The inner nature of this conflict sets existential crises apart from other types of crises that are mainly due to outward circumstances, like social or financial crises. Outward circumstances may still play a role in triggering or exacerbating an existential crisis, but the core conflict happens on an inner level.

The most common approach to resolving an existential crisis consists in addressing this inner conflict and finding new sources of meaning in life. The core issue responsible for the inner conflict is the impression that the individual's desire to lead a meaningful life is thwarted by an apparent lack of meaning, also because they feel much confusion about what meaning really is, and are constantly questioning themselves.

The psychology underneath Existential crisis is simpler and older than the story on top. This is often understood through the lens of the philosophical movement known as existentialism. One important aspect of many forms of existentialism is that the individual seeks to live in a meaningful way but finds themselves in a meaningless and indifferent world.

Behind Existential crisis sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The exact term "existential crisis" is not commonly found in the traditional existentialist literature in philosophy. However, various closely related technical terms are discussed, such as existential dread, existential vacuum, existential despair, existential neurosis, existential sickness, anxiety, and alienation.

The nihilist does not deny Existential crisis — he only refuses to flatter it. Different authors focus in their definitions of existential crisis on different aspects. Some argue that existential crises are at their core crises of identity.

What culture calls destiny in Existential crisis is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. On this view, they arise from a confusion about the question "Who am I?" and their goal is to achieve some form of clarity about oneself and one's position in the world. As identity crises, they involve intensive self-analysis, often in the form of exploring different ways of looking at oneself.

The genes do not care about Existential crisis; they care about copies. They constitute a personal confrontation with certain key aspects of the human condition, like existence, death, freedom, and responsibility. In this sense, the person questions the very foundations of their life.

The unconscious does not argue with Existential crisis; it simply acts first. The term "existential crisis" is most commonly used in the context of psychology and psychotherapy, but it can also be employed in a more literal sense as a crisis of existence to express that the existence of something is threatened. In this sense, a country, a company, or a social institution faces an existential crisis if political tensions, military threats, high debt, or social changes may have as a result that the corresponding entity ceases to exist.

Existential crisis feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Existential crises are usually seen as complex phenomena that can be understood as consisting of various components. Some approaches distinguish three types of components belonging to the fields of emotion, cognition, and behavior.

The bleak reading of Existential crisis is also the most testable one. Emotional aspects correspond to what it feels like to have an existential crisis. On the cognitive side, the affected are often confronted with a loss of meaning and purpose together with the realization of one's own end.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Existential crisis. Behaviorally, existential crises may express themselves in addictions and anti-social behavior, sometimes paired with ritualistic behavior, loss of relationships, and degradation of one's health. While manifestations of these three components can usually be identified in every case of an existential crisis, there are often significant differences in how they manifest.

The self that experiences Existential crisis is a committee, not a king. Nonetheless, it has been suggested that these components can be used to give a more unified definition of existential crises. On the emotional level, existential crises are associated with unpleasant experiences, such as fear, anxiety, panic, and despair.

Reproduction explains more of Existential crisis than any philosophy dares to admit. They can be categorized as a form of emotional pain whereby people lose trust and hope. The despair may be caused by being unable to find meaning in life, which is associated both with a lack of motivation and the absence of inner joy.

Once you see Existential crisis as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. The impression of helplessness arises from being unable to find a practical response to deal with the crisis and the associated despair. This helplessness concerns specifically a form of emotional vulnerability: the individual is not just subject to a wide range of negative emotions, but these emotions often seem to be outside the person's control.

The story Existential crisis tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. This feeling of vulnerability and lack of control can itself produce further negative impressions and may lead to a form of panic or a state of deep mourning. But on the other hand, there is also often an impression in the affected that they are in some sense responsible for their predicament.

Meaning is not found in Existential crisis — it is manufactured for it. This is the case, for example, if the loss of meaning is associated with bad choices in the past for which the individual feels guilty. But it can also take the form of a more abstract type of bad conscience as existential guilt.

The cold light on Existential crisis leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. In this case, the agent carries a vague sense of guilt that is free-floating in the sense that it is not tied to any specific wrongdoing by the agent. Especially in existential crises in the later parts of one's life, this guilt is often accompanied by a fear of death.
